title: A retargetable delivery platform for genetic medicines across the body

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a modular platform for carrying genetic medicines into selected cell populations in a living organism, with targeting that can be changed while retaining a reusable delivery architecture. Its defining capability would be reliable retargeting across different tissues and cell types: getting enough functional payload into the intended cells while limiting harmful activity elsewhere. “Across the body” describes the intended breadth of retargeting, not a requirement to expose every cell simultaneously. This is a synthesis of the proposed concept, not an achieved capability.

Changing which genetic sequence a medicine acts on is distinct from changing which cells receive it. The supplied clinical report describes a hepatic platform in which shared components could include the lipid nanoparticle formulation and editor messenger RNA, while the guide RNA is customized to a patient's variant. That modularity supports patient-specific genetic targeting within liver-directed therapy; it does not demonstrate that the delivery system can be redirected to another cell population.

significance.text: Conditional significance: reliable retargeting would expand the range of selected cells in which genetic payloads could act, opening additional opportunities for experiments and therapeutic interventions in living organisms. A reusable architecture could also allow knowledge gained for one application to inform another, although the extent of that reuse would itself need demonstration. The revolutionary capability would be predictable access to different cell populations, rather than a separate delivery solution having to be established independently for every application.

Successful delivery would not by itself establish disease reversal. The delivered medicine must produce an appropriate biological change, and that change must yield a clinically useful outcome at an acceptable risk. The supplied CPS1 report describes early clinical improvements with incomplete biochemical correction, illustrating why delivery, molecular correction and disease benefit must be evaluated separately. Its discussion of possible applications to hundreds of hepatic inborn errors of metabolism is a prospective opportunity, not a demonstrated range of treatments.

Scope limitation: neither the proposed concept nor the supplied single report establishes a universal carrier for every tissue, payload or disease. The evidence also does not provide a current comparison against the best available delivery methods across organs. Claims that particular populations remain inaccessible, or that this platform would outperform the delivery frontier in November 2026, therefore remain unestablished by this record.

missing_breakthrough.text: Proposed engineering requirements: the missing capability is reproducible control over where a genetic payload goes and whether it functions after reaching its destination. A platform must reach the selected population, enter enough of its cells, deliver an adequate functional dose, produce effects for an appropriate duration and limit unwanted effects elsewhere. These are distinct requirements: detecting a carrier in a tissue would not by itself show useful intracellular delivery, and useful delivery would not by itself show therapeutic benefit. The supplied evidence does not establish this full set of requirements across payload types.

The concrete unresolved extension is from the reported hepatocyte-directed approach to independent delivery targeting in other populations, such as neurons, muscle cells and blood-forming stem cells. Those are proposed test populations, not populations shown by this report to be reached or to resist all existing methods. Establishing the extension would require evidence about functional delivery, dose, specificity, unwanted activity and safety in each population. The supplied article supports the importance of these assessments within its hepatic application but does not characterize the tissue-specific barriers or solutions for those other targets.

Further engineering synthesis: a convincing modular platform must establish which components can remain shared and which must change when delivery is retargeted. It must also show whether targeting performance survives changes in dose, recipient and payload. Appropriate duration must be defined for the application; a durable biological outcome and prolonged exposure to an active genetic medicine are different properties. The present record supplies no general solution or quantitative design rules for these questions.

current_state.text: Musunuru, Grandinette, Wang and colleagues reported Patient-Specific In Vivo Gene Editing to Treat a Rare Genetic Disease online on 15 May 2025, DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2504747. The published clinical report describes a customized lipid-nanoparticle-delivered base-editing therapy directed to hepatocytes in one infant with neonatal-onset CPS1 deficiency. It is an early clinical demonstration of individualized liver-directed genetic medicine, not a demonstration of delivery across multiple organs.

Over seven weeks after the first infusion, the patient tolerated increased dietary protein and a reduced nitrogen-scavenger dose. These observations indicate early clinical benefit within a single-patient report. Liver biopsy was deferred, so corrective editing was not directly measured in the patient. The clinical observations should therefore be distinguished from direct measurement of the intended molecular correction. The short follow-up does not establish long-term safety or efficacy, and the authors explicitly called for longer observation.

The supplied review assessed the complete nine-page main article; supplementary appendices were not supplied. Its conclusions do not depend on interpreting extracted figure graphics. The article's discussion of shared delivery and editor components establishes a platform-development rationale, while its broader hepatic applications remain prospective. Neither cross-organ retargeting nor performance in neurons, muscle or blood-forming stem cells is established by this report.

Evidence coverage limitation: no subsequent-development assessment was supplied. The May 2025 result can be described at its reported date, but the record cannot establish the platform's frontier status or whether the broader delivery challenge remained open through 1 November 2026. This gap does not invalidate the dated clinical result.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independently retarget a modular platform to several prespecified difficult cell populations in large animals while delivering the same standardized genetic payload. Identify which components remain shared and which change between targets. Define a therapeutically meaningful level of functional delivery for each application before testing, and measure both the proportion of intended cells reached and the resulting biological activity. These are proposed criteria, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Retarget one standardized payload across several difficult large-animal cell populations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evaluation: measure cell-type specificity, delivery to unintended populations, unintended genetic activity where relevant, safety and outcomes over a prespecified duration. Distinguish carrier localization, functional payload delivery, molecular change and physiological benefit. The study should make clear whether an outcome persists after payload activity subsides and whether performance is reproducible across recipients and independently reproduced experiments.
completion_criteria.label: Report specificity, safety and reproducible outcomes over a prespecified duration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: success with several populations and one payload would establish demonstrated breadth only across those tested conditions. Additional payloads, doses and recipient settings would require further validation; finite testing cannot establish literal universality. Human studies across organs would be needed to establish clinical generality, with safety and therapeutic benefit evaluated for each intended use.
completion_criteria.label: State demonstrated delivery limits and human validation needed for clinical generality

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: GEN-01, “A predictive, causal map of the genome’s regulatory code,” and GEN-11, “Predicting genetic interactions across backgrounds and environments,” concern predicting what a genetic intervention will do. GEN-04 concerns getting the intervention into selected cells. Better prediction could guide payload selection and interpretation of outcomes, while delivery alone would not resolve regulatory causality or context-dependent genetic effects.

Roster-based synthesis: GEN-03, “Precise, programmable replacement of large genomic regions in existing cells,” overlaps most directly through the need to deliver genome-modifying machinery. Precise replacement and successful delivery are separate capabilities. GEN-02, “Design and construct complex eukaryotic genomes to specification,” concerns genome design and construction; a retargetable carrier would not itself establish either capability or the ability to deliver an entire constructed genome.

Roster-based synthesis: GEN-08, “Reconstructing an organism’s cell divisions and histories from inherited molecular marks,” could overlap with delivery when introducing molecular marking systems into selected cells. Delivering a marking payload would not establish accurate recording or reconstruction of cell histories. GEN-05, “General laws of environmentally induced, sequence-independent inheritance,” instead concerns the mechanisms and predictability of inheritance without sequence change; cell targeting would not establish those laws.

Roster-based synthesis: GEN-06, “Transferable clonal seed reproduction across major crops,” and GEN-07, “Predictably controllable inheritance in wild populations,” concern reproduction and inheritance across generations. Genetic delivery could be an enabling step in some implementations, but delivering a payload to cells does not demonstrate clonal seed reproduction, predictable population inheritance or control of spread. Those remain distinct innovations.

Roster-based synthesis: GEN-09, “An autonomous, evolvable expanded genetic alphabet,” concerns the operation and inheritance of an expanded information system. GEN-10, “A testable reconstruction of the origin and fixation of the genetic code,” concerns a historical and mechanistic explanation of the genetic code. Neither follows from retargetable delivery, even if delivery methods eventually assist experiments relevant to them.

unresolved_issues: The supplied record does not establish developments after the May 2025 report or the broader delivery frontier through 1 November 2026.
The tissue-specific barriers and comparative performance of delivery methods for neurons, muscle and blood-forming stem cells are not established by the supplied source.
Corrective editing was not directly measured in the reported patient; longer-term clinical safety and efficacy are not established by the seven-week observations.
Supplementary appendices were not supplied to the review, limiting assessment of evidence contained outside the main article.

The platform architecture, allowable targeting-component changes, target populations, payload, functional thresholds and follow-up duration for a convincing retargeting demonstration remain to be specified.
The extent to which successful targeting would transfer across payloads, doses and recipients remains an empirical question.

brief.title: Genetic medicines that can be sent to chosen cells
possible: Patients could receive genetic medicines directed to selected cells in different parts of the body. Researchers could change a medicine’s cellular destination while keeping a shared delivery system, getting enough medicine into the intended cells while limiting harmful activity elsewhere.
why: Reliable delivery would give researchers and doctors access to more cell populations for experiments and treatments. A reusable carrier could let lessons from one application help another, reducing the need to develop a separate delivery system for every use.

sources.who: K. Musunuru, S.A. Grandinette, X. Wang and colleagues
sources.showed: They treated one infant with a rare metabolic disease using tiny fat-based carriers to deliver a medicine designed to correct a genetic error in liver cells. The patient tolerated more dietary protein and needed less medication.
sources.quote:
In the 7 weeks after the initial 
infusion, the patient was able to receive an increased amount of dietary protein 
and a reduced dose of a nitrogen-scavenger medication to half the starting dose, 
without unacceptable adverse events and despite viral illnesses.
sources.cited_for: The study supports individualized genetic treatment directed to the liver.
sources.not_established: Changing the genetic error a medicine targets does not establish that its carrier can be redirected to other cell types.

sources.who: Moore Z. Chen, Daniel Yuen and colleagues
sources.showed: They attached antibodies, proteins that recognize cellular targets, to fat-based carriers holding messenger RNA, instructions for making proteins. These carriers efficiently targeted T cells, a type of immune cell, in living animals.
sources.quote: These precisely targeted LNPs showed highly efficient in vivo targeting to T cells, with minimal delivery to other immune cells.
sources.cited_for: The study supports selective delivery using an adaptable antibody attachment system.
sources.not_established: It does not establish reliable retargeting across several organs or cell populations.

sources.who: Theresa L. Hunter and colleagues at Capstan Therapeutics and collaborators
sources.showed: They delivered genetic instructions that turned selected T cells into cells equipped to attack a chosen target. Treatment controlled tumors in mice carrying human cells and depleted B cells, another immune cell type, in monkeys.
sources.quote:
These tLnPs 
reprogrammed CD8+ T cells in both healthy donor and 
autoimmune patient samples, and in vivo dosing resulted in 
tumor control in humanized mice and B cell depletion in 
cynomolgus monkeys.
sources.cited_for: The study connects selective delivery to biological effects in animals.
sources.not_established: It does not establish a shared delivery system that works across unrelated cell populations or clinical benefit in humans.

shown: Researchers have demonstrated individualized liver treatment in a patient and selective immune-cell delivery in animals. These are steps toward choosing where genetic medicines act, but no shared system has demonstrated the proposed breadth of retargeting.
missing: A shared carrier must deliver the same genetic cargo at useful levels to several selected cell populations in large animals.
Delivery must remain selective, safe and reproducible over a defined period, with unwanted activity measured.
Human studies across organs must establish safety and therapeutic benefit for each intended use.

milestones.label: A shared carrier reaches several difficult cell populations
milestones.explanation: Large-animal tests would have to deliver the same cargo to several predefined difficult cell populations, measuring reach and useful activity. This would establish which carrier parts can stay shared when destinations change.

milestones.label: Selective, safe effects last and can be reproduced
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to measure intended and unwanted activity, safety and outcomes over a predefined period, with independent reproduction. This would distinguish reliable biological effects from simply finding a carrier in tissue.

milestones.label: Delivery limits and human benefits are established
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to define tested limits across cargo, doses and recipients, then establish safety and benefit across organs in humans. This would show how broadly the system applies without claiming it works everywhere.

uncertain: The infant’s corrective genetic changes were not directly measured, and long-term safety and benefit remain unknown.
It remains unclear how well targeting would transfer between genetic cargos, doses and recipients.
Which carrier parts may change, what counts as enough delivery and how long effects should last still need definition.

page.title: Programmable in vivo delivery of genome editors
page.definition: A delivery system can be reprogrammed to carry genome editors—tools that change DNA—to at least three distinct cell types, tissues or organs in living animals. Independent large-animal testing establishes delivery and editing performance against published efficiencies for those targets.

goal.need: An analysis of Orphanet data from 1 October 2018 identified 6,172 rare diseases, including 4,440 classified as genetic. Genetic diseases affect different tissues; the NIH Somatic Cell Genome Editing Consortium identifies delivery as a principal obstacle to genome-editing therapies and seeks translation across tissues and diseases.

figures.caption: Rare diseases in the Orphanet dataset of 1 October 2018
figures.note: These are disease counts, not patient counts or estimates of eligibility for genome editing.

statements.body: NIH Somatic Cell Genome Editing Consortium
statements.quote: genome-editing technology to a wide range of tissues and diseases
statements.context: The consortium identifies accelerating translation of this technology as its overarching goal.

statements.body: National Institutes of Health, Office of Strategic Coordination
statements.quote: Programmable delivery systems that could target specific tissues or cell types (e.g., stem cells)
statements.context: The request for information lists this capability among strategic delivery gaps that a prize competition could address.

completion.title: One programmable system passes independent large-animal delivery and editing tests at three distinct targets.
completion.criterion: Meet NIH TARGETED Challenge Target Area 1 requirements: reprogram one delivery system for at least three distinct cell types, tissues or organs; demonstrate delivery and editing at least as efficient as published methods for those targets; establish the biological mechanism of programmability, biodistribution and administration route; demonstrate a safety profile consistent with gene-therapy or genome-editing delivery systems intended for humans; and demonstrate successful delivery and editing through NIH-supported independent large-animal evaluation. Systems targeting only the central nervous system belong to Target Area 2.
completion.set_by: National Institutes of Health, TARGETED Challenge, Target Area 1 final requirements and Phase 3b evaluation criteria
completion.threshold_quote: Be programmable and target at least three distinct and different cell(s), tissue types, and/or organs.
completion.basis: TARGETED supplies an external operational test for programmable delivery, including target-specific efficiency comparisons and independent large-animal evaluation. Its endpoint establishes a delivery capability; clinical benefit remains an application-specific question. Changing a guide RNA within an unchanged liver-directed formulation, as discussed in the CPS1 report, does not establish retargeting between cell populations.

milestones.title: A delivery system demonstrates genome editing in the laboratory developing it.
milestones.criterion: Establish delivery-mediated editing as laboratory proof of principle, the initial SCGE development stage. The report published on 15 May 2025 demonstrated up to 42% corrective editing in whole-liver samples from engineered mice receiving k-abe lipid nanoparticles: two mice at each of 0.1, 1.0 and 3.0 mg/kg, with eight liver samples per mouse. Its subsequent treatment of one infant provided clinical observations, but no liver biopsy measurement of editing.
milestones.set_by: NIH Somatic Cell Genome Editing Consortium, published development pathway, initial laboratory stage

milestones.title: One delivery system is reprogrammed to deliver an editor and edit at least three distinct targets.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate the programmability component of TARGETED Target Area 1: delivery and editing at three or more distinct cellular or tissue targets, with a known biological mechanism linking platform modifications to targeting. Cheng and colleagues reported mouse liver-, lung- and spleen-directed SORT lipid nanoparticles on 6 April 2020. Cas9 messenger RNA and guide RNA activated an editing reporter with three mice per group: liver and lung at 2.5 mg total RNA/kg, assessed after 10 days; spleen at 4 mg/kg, assessed after 2 days. This establishes mouse retargeting, without the completion test’s independent large-animal validation.
milestones.set_by: National Institutes of Health, TARGETED Challenge, Target Area 1 programmability requirements
milestones.threshold_quote: Have a known biological mechanism for programmability

milestones.title: A delivery system’s editing activity is successfully validated by an independent small-animal testing centre.
milestones.criterion: An SCGE Small Animal Testing Center independently validates the technology outside its developer’s laboratory, meeting the programme’s prespecified efficacy milestones before large-animal testing. The SCGE Toolkit records independent mouse-liver validation of engineered virus-like particles carrying an adenine base editor: one dose of 5 × 10^11 particles produced a reported mean of 34.5% edited reads in the male group, with three listed replicate values. The undated dataset does not establish three-target retargeting.
milestones.set_by: NIH Somatic Cell Genome Editing Consortium, published independent-validation gate for progression to large-animal testing
milestones.threshold_quote: successful independent validation of the technology by an SATC

milestones.title: A programmable delivery system demonstrates effectiveness and readiness for independent large-animal testing.
milestones.criterion: Meet the TARGETED Phase 3a readiness gate: demonstrate effectiveness in prior in vivo studies supporting the proposed large-animal dose, administration route and any species-specific optimisation, with capacity to supply reagents at the required scale and quality. NCATS’s page updated on 5 September 2025 lists ten Target Area 1 Phase 2 winners selected using delivery and editing data. That preliminary-data selection does not establish passage of the Phase 3a readiness gate.
milestones.set_by: National Institutes of Health, TARGETED Challenge, Phase 3a review criteria and submission requirements, revision of 2 July 2025
milestones.threshold_quote: Final data demonstrating effectiveness of solution and readiness for large animal testing

not_found: No published independent large-animal result satisfying the complete three-target TARGETED test was found.
No universal numerical SCGE small-animal efficacy threshold or delivery-system safety cutoff was found.
No public TARGETED Phase 3a dataset establishing dose, route and scale-up readiness was found.

results.finding: K-abe lipid nanoparticles produced up to 42% whole-liver corrective editing in six engineered mice.
results.detail: Two mice received each of three doses; eight liver samples per mouse were sequenced. The infant’s liver was not biopsied to measure editing.
results.quote:
we observed up to 42% whole-liver cor -
rective editing

results.finding: Antibody-capturing LNPs targeted 1 cell type, T cells, in vivo; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The anti-Fc nanobody captures antibodies on the LNP surface, but the supplied text does not report delivery to three targets or genome editing.
results.quote: These precisely targeted LNPs showed highly efficient in vivo targeting to T cells, with minimal delivery to other immune cells.

results.finding: SORT lipid nanoparticles delivered Cas9 and edited three mouse organs: liver, lung and spleen; n=3 mice per group.
results.detail: Targeting changed with the added lipid’s properties and proportion. The authors reported that the precise biological mechanisms remained under investigation.
results.quote: These data indicate that the described methodology enables liver-, lung-, and spleen-specific CRISPR/Cas gene editing.

results.finding: Independent mouse-liver validation of eVLP-delivered ABE8e reported 34.5% edited reads in males, with three listed replicates.
results.detail: The SCGE Toolkit identifies the experiment as independent validation, but the source does not state the programme’s prespecified efficacy milestones or establish that they were met before large-animal testing. The number of mice is not specified.

results.finding: Zempleni’s milk-exosome delivery technology reportedly earned a Phase 3a win; sample size not reported.
results.detail: The university reports a Phase 3a win but does not describe the prior in vivo evidence, proposed large-animal dose or route, species-specific optimisation, or reagent supply capacity needed to establish the readiness criterion.
results.quote: Zempleni’s innovative strategy recently earned him a Phase 3a win in the National Institutes of Health’s Targeted Genome Editor Delivery Challenge, placing Nebraska in an elite group of research institutions and highlighting the potential for breakthroughs at the intersection of biomedical science and agriculture.
